topics.name: Source text and tokenization
topics.description: Source files are divided into lexical tokens, with whitespace and comments separating them.

topics.name: Character classes
topics.description: The lexical rules distinguish whitespace, printable characters, digits, and ASCII letters.

topics.name: Numeric literals
topics.description: Numerals, decimals, hexadecimal literals, and binary literals each have a prescribed spelling.

topics.name: String literals
topics.description: Double quotes delimit strings, and doubling an interior quote gives the language’s single lexical escape.

topics.name: Symbols and reserved words
topics.description: Symbols, keywords, and reserved words supply the names and fixed vocabulary of the language.

topics.name: S-expressions and constants
topics.description: Special constants and other atoms combine into possibly empty parenthesized S-expressions.

topics.name: Indexed identifiers
topics.description: Identifiers are symbols, optionally qualified by one or more numeral or symbol indices.

topics.name: Attribute syntax
topics.description: An attribute consists of a keyword with an optional special constant, symbol, or parenthesized list as its value.

topics.name: Sort expressions
topics.description: Sort expressions are identifiers, optionally applied to one or more sort expressions.

topics.name: Term grammar
topics.description: Terms combine constants, identifiers, applications, abstractions, quantifiers, local definitions, matches, and annotations.

topics.name: Variables and scope
topics.description: Local variable declarations associate names with terms or sorts and determine the scope of their occurrences.

topics.name: Pattern matching
topics.description: Flat constructor patterns, variable patterns, and wildcards describe the cases of a match expression.

topics.name: Term annotations
topics.description: Attributes attach additional information to a term without changing its logical meaning.

topics.name: Scripts and solver interaction
topics.description: Scripts sequence commands that control a solver and request its responses.

topics.name: Declarations and definitions
topics.description: Sort, datatype, constructor, selector, and function declarations describe the components introduced by commands.

topics.name: Command syntax and options
topics.description: Command productions specify their arguments, including option attributes and information flags.

passages.quote: Symbols are case sensitive. They are used mainly as operators or identifiers. Conven- tionally, arithmetic characters and the like are used, individually or in combination, as operator names; in contrast, alpha-numeric symbols, possibly with punctuation char- acters and underscores, are used as identifiers. But, as in LISP, this usage is only rec- ommended (for human readability), not prescribed. For additional flexibility, arbitrary sequences of whitespace and printable characters (except for | and \) enclosed in verti- cal bars are also allowed as symbols. Following Common Lisp’s conventions, enclosing a simple symbol in vertical bars does not produce a new symbol. This means for instance that abc and |abc| are the same symbol. Simple symbols starting with the character @ or . are reserved for solver use.4 Solvers can use them respectively as identifiers for abstract values and solver-generated function symbols other than abstract values.

passages.quote: Abstractly, terms are constructed out of constant symbols in the ⟨spec_constant ⟩ category (numerals, decimals, strings, etc.), variables, function symbols, five kinds of binders (introduced by the reserved words lambda, let, forall, exists, and match), and an annotation operator: the reserved word !. In its simplest form, a term is a special constant symbol, a variable, a function symbol, or the application of a function symbol to one or more terms. More complex terms include one or more binders. Concretely, a variable can be any ⟨symbol ⟩ , while a function symbol can be any ⟨identifier ⟩ (i.e., a symbol or an indexed symbol). As a consequence, contextual information is needed during parsing to know whether an identifier is to be treated as a variable or a function sym- bol. For variables, this information is provided by the binders let, lambda, forall, exists, and match, which are the only mechanism to introduce variables. Function symbols, in con- trast, are predefined, as explained later. Recall that every function symbol f is separately associated with one or more ranks, each specifying the sorts of f ’s arguments and result. To simplify sort checking, a function symbol in a term can be annotated with one of its result sorts τ. Such an annotated function symbol is a qualified identifier of the form (as f τ).

BSmtLibSpec.Regex.text: The formal definition treats a language as any set of finite byte sequences. Its operations express alternatives, concatenation, repetition and exclusion, as in Appendix B. It does not require a language to be regular in the automata-theoretic sense. The lexical rules are built with these operations; this declaration alone is not a recognition algorithm or a claim about computational complexity.

BSmtLibSpec.Regex.chars.text: This operation converts each character of a supplied string to one byte. For ASCII strings, including the punctuation and reserved words used in the grammar, the conversion preserves the character codes. It is not a general Unicode encoding procedure. The formal definition accepts other strings as inputs, so the stated ASCII use is a convention of the grammar rather than a restriction enforced by this operation.

BSmtLibSpec.Regex.plus.text: Repetition requires at least one matching part here, not necessarily at least one character. If the repeated language contains the empty sequence, repeating it one or more times also admits the empty sequence. In the numeral and keyword rules, the repeated parts are single characters, so their use of this operation does require nonempty text.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.SourceFile.text: Version 2.0 requires every byte in a source file to be below 128. For versions 2.5, 2.6 and 2.7, this particular condition imposes no restriction. It neither decodes Unicode nor establishes that an input is a valid encoding. Lexical and grammatical conditions are defined separately, and tokenisation does not automatically include this source-file condition.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.printableChar.text: The formal definition accepts one byte with value from 32 to 126 or from 128 to 255. This matches the bounded ranges printed in Appendix B. The main text instead speaks of Unicode characters from 128 onward. A character encoded in several bytes can pass the byte-based rules, but the formal definition does not decode or validate that encoding.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.comment.text: A comment begins with a semicolon and contains no line feed or carriage return before its terminating line-breaking character. The terminating character is part of the matched sequence. Whether the semicolon lies outside a string or quoted symbol is determined when the surrounding input is tokenised. A separate rule admits a final comment that reaches the end of input without a line break.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.commentAtEnd.text: This rule admits a semicolon followed by any number of bytes other than line feed or carriage return, with no terminating line break. It is used only for a comment at the end of input. The standard's main definition ends a comment at the first subsequent line-breaking character; accepting an unfinished final comment is an additional reading adopted by the formalization.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.whitespaceAtEnd.text: The end of input may contain ordinary whitespace followed by either nothing or a final semicolon comment without a line break. Ordinary whitespace already includes terminated comments and the four white space characters. This separate final-input rule is why a file can end inside a comment without being rejected by tokenisation.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.numeral.text: A numeral is either the single digit 0 or a nonempty string of decimal digits whose first digit is not 0. This is a lexical rule: it rejects leading zeroes such as 01 and does not attach a numerical interpretation. As the paper explains for special constants, the surrounding theory supplies their meaning when they occur as terms.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.decimal.text: A decimal consists of a numeral, a decimal point, zero or more zeroes, and a final numeral. Consequently there is at least one digit on each side of the point, and leading zeroes are allowed only in the fractional part. The definition recognises spelling; it does not interpret the token as a rational number, floating-point value or any other theory-specific object.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.string.text: String literals have opening and closing double quotes. Between them, the formal definition permits printable bytes and the four white space characters, with each internal double quote represented twice. A backslash has no escaping role in this rule. The same spelling rule is used for versions 2.5, 2.6 and 2.7; version 2.0 has a separate rule.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.unescape.text: Given the interior of a string literal, the formal definition replaces each pair of adjacent double quotes by one double quote and preserves every other byte. Removing the surrounding quotes is performed separately when token contents are obtained. This operation assumes the intended use on a recognised string interior; it does not itself test whether the input was a well-formed literal.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.string20.text: The earlier string rule recognises the version 2.0 use of backslashes, rather than the doubled quotation marks used in version 2.7. It admits printable bytes and white space inside the quotes, treating a backslash together with its following character as one part. The separate source-file condition supplies version 2.0's ASCII restriction. This historical rule should not be read as the rule for the present standard.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.unescape20.text: For the interior of a version 2.0 string, a backslash before a double quote or another backslash is removed. Other backslashes remain. The formal definition does not recognise or decode escapes such as a backslash followed by n. It is a historical decoding rule, used after stripping the enclosing quotes, and is not the version 2.7 doubled-quote convention.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.addedCommandNames.text: The formal definition lists commands when they first become available and later combines those lists across versions. It includes define-funs-rec from version 2.5 onward, and declare-sort-parameter and define-const in version 2.7. Appendix B's reserved-command list omits define-funs-rec, although the command appears in the command grammar and the main text says every command name is reserved.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.keyword.text: The formal definition accepts a colon followed by any nonempty sequence of letters, digits and the punctuation permitted in simple symbols. Thus a keyword may begin with a digit or use a reserved word after the colon. This follows the older rule and the paper's example :56, but is broader than the stated version 2.7 production requiring a simple symbol after the colon.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.simpleSymbol.text: A simple symbol is a nonempty sequence of ASCII letters, digits and the listed punctuation, with no initial digit and no spelling reserved by the selected version. Names beginning with @ or a dot are still recognised as symbols. Their restriction to solver use concerns where such names may be introduced; it is not imposed by this lexical definition.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.quotedSymbol.text: A quoted symbol has a vertical bar at each end and may contain printable bytes or white space in between, except for vertical bars and backslashes. Empty quoted symbols are permitted. This rule recognises their spelling only. Obtaining the symbol's name removes the enclosing bars, while the syntax representation separately remembers that the spelling was quoted.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Token.content.text: The formal definition removes the delimiters of strings and quoted symbols, decodes the appropriate string escapes, removes the colon of a keyword, and removes the #x or #b prefix of hexadecimal or binary literals. Other token text is preserved. These are conventions for what the parser receives; the declaration does not assign the logical meaning of a literal or establish symbol equality.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization.Delimit.text: After any token other than a parenthesis, the formalization requires the end of input or a following white space character, parenthesis or semicolon. This prevents adjacent tokens from being split arbitrarily: a decimal such as 1.5 remains one token, and a quoted string immediately followed by an unquoted symbol is rejected. The standard describes whitespace's separating role but does not explicitly state this complete delimitation rule.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization.From.text: The input is split into recognised tokens separated by whitespace and comments, beginning at a supplied byte offset. Each token's position includes the preceding whitespace. Non-parenthesis tokens obey the formalization's additional delimiter rule, and a final comment may end without a newline. This relation describes tokenisation; it does not enforce Unicode encoding validity or the separate source-file restriction for version 2.0.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization.text: Tokenisation starts at byte offset zero and applies the version-dependent lexical rules across the entire input. Spaces and comments are omitted from the token list. The formalization also requires delimiters after non-parenthesis tokens and accepts a final comment without a newline. These choices make the relation more specific than the paper's statement that whitespace separates tokens.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization.Exactly.text: In addition to ordinary tokenisation from an offset, this condition requires a last token whose end coincides with the end of the input. The token list therefore cannot be empty, and no trailing whitespace or comment is permitted. It is useful for cutting a script immediately after a command's closing parenthesis before reading subsequent input in another version.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Properties.Unique.text: This declaration defines the requirement that two tokenisations of the same input under the same version must give exactly the same tokens. It is a condition about the formal lexical rules, rather than a proof that they satisfy it. The authors' proof that the rules satisfy it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Properties.Determine.text: A list of tokens is determined by the current input prefix when every tokenisation of every valid continuation begins with that list. The empty list always qualifies. If no continuation can be tokenised, every list satisfies the condition vacuously, so the formalization uses a separate condition requiring that the prefix admit a valid continuation when describing actual token delivery.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Properties.ReadsOnIt.text: The requirement states that tokenising from an arbitrary offset gives exactly a tokenisation from zero with every token's position shifted by that offset. This concerns source positions, not lexical meaning. It supports reading successive file segments separately. The declaration defines the desired equivalence; it does not itself prove that equivalence for the lexical rules.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Symbol.text: A symbol is represented by its name together with a flag remembering whether vertical bars were used. The standard treats a simple symbol and its quoted spelling as the same name. This representation preserves their different spellings, so equality of the stored representations is a stronger distinction than equality of names. A comparison of language-level names must ignore the quoting flag.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.SyntaxToken.ofToken.text: This conversion removes source offsets and turns a recognised lexical token into the token used by the grammar. Strings are decoded, symbol names lose their surrounding bars, and binary and hexadecimal literals lose their prefixes. Whether a symbol was quoted is retained. The conversion presupposes that lexical recognition has already established the token's permitted spelling.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SExpr.Valid.text: This condition restricts reserved-word atoms to versions 2.6 and 2.7 and requires the word to belong to that version's reserved set. Lists must satisfy the same condition recursively. Other atoms are admitted without further tests here because their spelling belongs to the lexical stage. The declaration supplies version restrictions, not the whole definition of S-expression syntax.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Index.Valid.text: Numeral indices are admitted in every supported version; symbol indices are admitted from version 2.5 onward. This condition does not check the characters of the numeral or symbol. The choice of 2.5 follows the paper's change log, although Appendix A's historical note gives 2.6. Both alternatives are available for the version 2.7 page.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Sort.Valid.text: A sort satisfies this condition when its identifier has permitted indices and all its argument sorts satisfy the same grammatical condition. It does not consult a signature, check the declared arity of a sort symbol, or distinguish a sort parameter from a sort constructor. The paper's rules for well-formed sorts require that additional information.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.AttributeValue.text: Attribute values have three represented forms: a special constant, a symbol, or a list of S-expressions. A keyword or reserved word cannot appear as a lone value, though either may occur inside a list when the version permits it. This follows the displayed production; the prose description as S-expressions other than keywords is less restrictive about reserved words.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.QualIdentifier..text: The formal condition requires the identifier's indices and any attached sort to satisfy their grammatical conditions in the selected version. It does not determine the symbol's rank or check that the attached sort is one of its possible result sorts. Those are requirements of well-sortedness in the paper, which are not supplied by this grammatical condition.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern.Valid.text: A single symbol or wildcard must be available in the selected version. A constructor pattern must have at least one argument, and every argument must be a permitted symbol or wildcard. The formal condition does not check constructor names, argument sorts, distinct pattern variables or coverage of a datatype's constructors. These are additional requirements in the paper.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.Valid.text: The formal definition enforces nonempty lists where the grammar uses one or more repetitions, permits match from version 2.6 and lambda from version 2.7, and applies grammatical conditions recursively. It does not check variable scope, distinct let variables, sort compatibility, exhaustive match cases or the logical meaning of annotations. A term satisfying it is grammatically admissible at this stage, not necessarily well sorted.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.text: The represented application form has a qualified identifier in function position, as in the main term production. Section 3.9 additionally permits omitting @ when applying any term of monomorphic map sort, allowing a term in that position. That broader shorthand is not represented here; it can instead be written with explicit @. The representation also allows empty lists, with required nonemptiness checked separately.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.tokens.text: The formal definition writes the tokens of every represented term, including applications, let expressions, abstractions, quantifiers, matches and annotations. Lists may be empty in the representation, so writing tokens alone does not establish the grammar's nonemptiness conditions. The separate grammatical condition supplies those restrictions. Neither operation assigns logical meaning to the resulting term.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.ValidBindi.text: This condition applies the grammatical term restrictions to the defining term in each let binding. It imposes no nonemptiness condition on the whole list and does not require the variable names to be distinct. Nonemptiness is handled by the enclosing let-expression rule. The standard's parallel substitution semantics and distinct-name requirement are not established here.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.ValidCases.text: For each match case, the formal condition requires the pattern and its body to satisfy their grammatical restrictions in the selected version. It does not require the list of cases to be nonempty; that is handled by the enclosing match-expression rule. It also does not establish exhaustive matching, distinct variables, compatible sorts or the semantics of choosing a case.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.DatatypeDec.Val.text: The datatype declaration must contain at least one constructor, and each constructor's selector sorts must satisfy their grammatical conditions. This does not establish the paper's requirements on distinct names, matching numbers of sort parameters, permitted recursive occurrences or well-foundedness of mutually recursive datatypes. Those restrictions need information beyond the syntax of this declaration.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.FunctionDec.Val.text: This condition checks the grammatical form of each parameter sort and the result sort. It does not establish that those sorts exist in the current signature, that parameters have distinct names, or that the function name is fresh. The formal definition is one part of recognising declaration syntax, rather than the full test required before introducing a function.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.FunctionDef.Val.text: The parameter sorts, result sort and defining term must satisfy their grammatical conditions. The definition does not check that the term has the declared result sort, that its variables are in scope, or that recursive references are permitted. In particular, the difference between ordinary and recursive function definitions is not settled by this condition alone.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.Valid.text: The command must be available in the selected version and satisfy the grammar's nonemptiness, list-length and recursive syntax conditions. Version 2.7 admits arbitrary terms as check-sat-assuming arguments; versions 2.5 and 2.6 admit only propositional literals. These conditions do not require Boolean assumptions, maintain an assertion stack, enforce solver execution modes or determine command responses.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.tokens.text: The formal definition writes the tokens of each represented command, including names, arguments and parentheses. It also represents the older literal-only form of check-sat-assuming separately from the version 2.7 form with term arguments. The token sequence alone does not establish version availability, the required list lengths, or the operational effects of executing a command.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsSExpr.text: A token sequence represents a specified S-expression exactly when that expression satisfies the selected version's grammatical condition and writing it yields those tokens. The relation is about tokens already supplied to the grammar, not arbitrary source characters. In particular, recognising legal spellings and decoding quoted literals are responsibilities of the preceding lexical stage.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsSort.text: A token sequence represents a specified sort when the sort satisfies the selected version's grammatical condition and is written by exactly that sequence. This matches the displayed syntax production at the token level. It does not establish that the sort's symbols are declared or applied with their declared arities; those are separate semantic requirements.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsTerm.text: A token sequence represents a specified term when that term satisfies the grammatical restrictions for the selected version and writing it yields those tokens. The condition combines the term forms with their required nonempty lists. It does not require a signature or prove well-sortedness, variable scope, substitution laws or logical equivalences between term forms.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsCommand.text: This relation combines the token sequence of a command with the command's version-dependent grammatical conditions. It therefore includes the grammar's nonempty and equal-length list requirements. It describes a recognised command, not its execution: no assertion stack, model, satisfiability result or solver response is part of the relation.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.modeAft.text: The formalization treats a set-info declaration of :smt-lib-version as changing the reading version after the command's closing parenthesis. Exit stops all further reading, and reset leaves the reading version unchanged. An unsupported or malformed version declaration has no allowed continuation. These are the formalization's file-reading choices; they do not define the solver's complete operational state.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.File.text: A file is read as successive commands, with lexical rules chosen by the version in force for each command. Version declarations take effect after their closing parenthesis. Once exit is read, the remaining characters are unrestricted and are not parsed. This is a relation describing the formalization's reading policy; it does not impose all semantic constraints on standard scripts or official benchmarks.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Script.text: Each command must satisfy the grammatical conditions of the version in force where it begins. A version declaration changes that version for later commands, and a command that stops reading may occur only last. The relation does not enforce well-sortedness, solver execution modes or the official benchmark requirement that version metadata occur exactly once as the first command.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Properties.SExprsOne.text: The requirement states that two S-expressions satisfying the grammatical conditions of the same version must be identical if their token sequences are identical. The version is held fixed because different versions can admit different forms. This declaration defines unambiguity as a proposition; the authors' proof of it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Properties.Attribute.text: The requirement states that two attributes satisfying the grammatical conditions of the same version must be identical if their token sequences are identical. The version is held fixed because different versions can admit different forms. This declaration defines unambiguity as a proposition; the authors' proof of it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Properties.SortsOneT.text: The requirement states that two sorts satisfying the grammatical conditions of the same version must be identical if their token sequences are identical. The version is held fixed because different versions can admit different forms. This declaration defines unambiguity as a proposition; the authors' proof of it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Properties.TermsOneT.text: The requirement states that two terms satisfying the grammatical conditions of the same version must be identical if their token sequences are identical. The version is held fixed because different versions can admit different forms. This declaration defines unambiguity as a proposition; the authors' proof of it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Properties.CommandsO.text: The requirement states that two commands satisfying the grammatical conditions of the same version must be identical if their token sequences are identical. The version is held fixed because different versions can admit different forms. This declaration defines unambiguity as a proposition; the authors' proof of it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Properties.FilesUniq.text: This requirement says that, for a fixed initial version, one character sequence cannot be read as two different command sequences. It includes changes of reading version within the file and the rule that exit ends reading. The declaration defines the uniqueness property. The authors' proof of it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Properties.CommandsH.text: This requirement starts with a segment whose tokenisation ends exactly at a complete command. It asks that all of those tokens be ready for delivery without waiting for another character. A command ends with a closing parenthesis, which needs no following delimiter. The declaration states the desired property; the authors' proof that token delivery satisfies it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.locate.text: Positions use a byte offset, a line number and a column number, all counted from zero. Only line feed increases the line number; carriage return remains an ordinary byte for location tracking even though it terminates comments. Columns count bytes since the last line feed. These are location conventions of the implementation specification, not a Unicode character-position model.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.HandoverReady.text: A token list is ready when every valid continuation must preserve that list and each non-parenthesis token has a following character already in the input. The latter condition ensures that its required delimiter has arrived. A quoted symbol can therefore already be determined while still awaiting delivery. Viability of the current input is considered separately in the surrounding delivery conditions.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.HandoverMaximal.text: The formal condition requires a ready token list whose length is at least that of every other ready list. It describes delivering everything that can already be delivered without waiting for more input. If the input has no valid continuation, the underlying condition for determined tokens is vacuous; the specification therefore applies this notion to the longest prefix that still admits a continuation.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.FailsCorrectly.text: Before the input ends, failure is required exactly when no continuation can produce a tokenisation. After it ends, failure is required exactly when the complete input has no tokenisation. Thus an unfinished quoted string may remain acceptable while further input is possible. This declaration specifies the error behavior a lexer must satisfy; it does not prove that an implementation satisfies it.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.HandsOverMaximal.text: Given a longest input prefix that still admits a valid continuation, the required output is exactly the maximal ready token list for that prefix, with source locations measured in the original input. No end-of-input marker is included in this condition. It defines expected output on incomplete or invalid input, rather than establishing that a particular lexer produces it.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.Correct.text: A lexer meets this definition when its error flag and delivered tokens satisfy the stated requirements for every supported version, every division of the input into pieces, and both ended and unfinished input. The condition includes waiting for sufficient delimiters and rejecting impossible continuations. It is a definition of lexer correctness, not a theorem establishing correctness of an implementation.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.Sequential.text: The required consistency is that adding more input pieces cannot retract previously delivered tokens or undo a failure. The same must hold when an unfinished input is marked as ended. This expresses monotone progress for a streaming lexer. The declaration defines that condition; the authors derive it from the broader correctness requirement in a proof shown as source with this page, not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.WholeInputCorrect.text: For input marked as ended, successful delivery of a specified list is required to be equivalent to that list consisting of a valid tokenisation followed by the end-of-input marker. This is a complete-input specification, independent of how the input was divided into pieces. The declaration defines the equivalence; it does not prove a lexer implements it.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.ComposesAtClose.text: The requirement concerns a tokenised prefix ending exactly with a closing parenthesis. All its tokens must already be ready, and any continuation must tokenise as the original tokens followed by a separately tokenised suffix with shifted positions. This gives the intended basis for changing reading versions between commands. The declaration defines the requirement; the authors' proof of it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.Consumer.BreaksAtEnd.text: The recipient of tokens must return a result or report an error when it receives the end-of-input marker; it must not ask to continue. Later correctness conditions for lexer interaction assume this obligation. The requirement concerns the recipient, not the lexer, and the declaration does not establish that every recipient necessarily obeys it.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.AfterBreak.text: Once a recipient returns a result before the input ends, the formal relation describes what follows. A further ordinary entry causes a trailing-input error; the end-of-input marker confirms the result. If no entry is ready, a lexical failure invalidates it, otherwise it remains pending. These are specified interaction rules rather than properties of an SMT solver's logical answers.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.ResetsAtEnd.text: After a previous input finishes successfully, the requirement makes processing the next input identical to starting with a fresh lexer in the original version. This resets reading state between separate inputs. It is distinct from the SMT-LIB reset command inside a script, which the formalization leaves in the current reading version. The declaration defines the condition, not its proof.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.CorrectWithConsumers.text: This definition combines three obligations: correct tokenisation with an unrestricted recipient, the specified interaction with every recipient that stops by the end of input, and a fresh state after a completed input. It covers early return, recipient errors and reading-version requests. It does not establish implementation correctness or define the logical semantics of the commands being read.

BSmtLibSpec.Lexer.DropsHeldOnError.text: For a lexer that reports errors and resumes, this requirement says that any error after a recipient has returned a result removes that pending result. The result can therefore be confirmed only if no later error has occurred. The specification does not describe which tokens are produced during error recovery, and this declaration is not a proof of recovery correctness.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.VersionPolicy.text: A reading policy lists the supported versions that a script may declare and may place a limit on the number of declarations. It does not require version information to be the first command, nor enforce the other metadata rules for official benchmarks. These are configurable parser restrictions; the standard's benchmark convention is a separate requirement.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.VersionPolicy.check.text: When the policy limits the number of version declarations, the formal definition first tests whether the allowed number has already been reached. Only then does it test whether the requested version is permitted. A declaration violating both restrictions is reported as exceeding the count. This specifies a parser policy and its error priority, not a rule imposed by the standard on every script.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.Received.Of.text: For a reserved-word token, this condition requires membership in the reserved set of the selected version. Every other token or end-of-input item is accepted by this condition. It is therefore only the version-dependent reserved-word check, relying on the lexical stage for permitted spellings. It does not establish that the item is legal at its current grammatical position.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.term.text: The formal definition specifies the order of callbacks when a term is read. Subterms are processed before the callback for their containing form; local scopes are announced before their bodies and closed afterward. The recipient chooses the returned values and may fail. No logical interpretation, substitution operation or well-sortedness test is fixed by this callback schedule.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.bindings.text: For a let expression, the defining terms are read in order before the callback that opens the scope of the new variables. This ordering allows a recipient to implement the paper's parallel binding convention. The formal definition does not itself maintain an environment, require distinct variable names, or prove that evaluating the expression agrees with simultaneous substitution.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.cases.text: Each match case is read by taking its pattern, announcing a new case scope, reading the body, and closing that scope. The already processed scrutinee is passed to the relevant callbacks. This supplies a useful order for implementing case checks. It does not verify constructor coverage, infer pattern-variable sorts or establish the semantics of the selected case.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.attributeTh.text: After an attribute keyword has been read, the next token may be needed to determine whether the attribute has a value. If a value is present, the callback occurs after that value and before the following token. Without a value, the following token is processed first. This specifies callback timing and does not assign meaning to particular attribute names.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.datatype.text: The formal definition announces a datatype's sort parameters once the input distinguishes the parametric form from the form without parameters. It then processes the sorts in its constructor selectors before completing the declaration. This ordering provides information needed by a recipient performing checks. It does not itself enforce well-foundedness, parameter counts or the restrictions on recursive datatype occurrences.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.recursiveBo.text: Each recursive function body is accompanied by its previously processed signature. A start notification occurs when the body's first token arrives, before processing that token; an end notification follows the last token. This describes when a recipient can enter and leave the relevant context. It does not prove that the body is well sorted or gives the required defining equation.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.command.text: The formal definition processes a command's tokens and arguments, then sends the appropriate command notification after its closing parenthesis. Ordinary and recursive function definitions use different scope notifications. A set-info command is reported here without changing the reading version; that change is performed by the surrounding script traversal. Executing the command's solver action is left to the recipient.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.switchVersi.text: Once a version declaration is complete, the requested version is tested against the policy. The token producer is then asked to switch and may refuse; only after success is the new version announced to the recipient. This specifies the order of implementation requests. It does not establish that version changes are required by the operational semantics of set-info.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.commands.text: Commands are processed in order. After a supported version declaration, the reading policy is applied and the version changes for subsequent input. After exit, the producer is asked to discard the rest and the parser receives only the end-of-input marker. A malformed or unsupported version declaration is rejected after its closing parenthesis. These rules concern reading a script, not executing its logical operations.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Properties.TakesItsTo.text: The requirement says that traversing any grammatically admitted script must record exactly its token sequence followed by the appropriate end-of-input item, both at arrival and at processing. The hypothesis is membership in the formal script relation, with its version and exit rules. The declaration defines this property of traversal; it is not the theorem proving it.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Properties.CallsDeter.text: For two admitted scripts with the same initial version, identical callback sequences are required to imply identical command sequences. The condition concerns the information preserved in notifications, rather than the meaning or execution of those commands. Whitespace is already absent at this stage. The declaration defines the reconstruction requirement; the authors' proof of it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Properties.PlacementD.text: For two admitted scripts with the same initial version and the same first $n$ input items, the requirement makes their events before the next arrival and processing point agree. A streaming parser should therefore need no future tokens to choose those earlier callbacks. This is the stated dependency condition; the authors' proof of it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Properties.FollowsThe.text: On every prefix of an admissible command input, the parser must produce exactly the reference events up to the next arrival. It waits on proper prefixes and finishes, or rejects an unsupported version declaration, when the specified input ends. This is a condition on an arbitrary parser's observed behavior. It does not itself prove that a concrete parser follows the reference traversal.

BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Properties.RejectsFir.text: This requirement covers the first token that prevents an otherwise admissible prefix from extending to a script. It assumes the lexer supplies reserved words allowed by the active version and honours a request to discard input after exit. The parser must reject that item with the prescribed earlier callbacks. The declaration defines the obligation rather than proving an implementation satisfies it.

BSmtLibSpec.Reader.ReadsFiles.text: For every input admitted by the formal file relation, this condition requires the reader to finish after end of input and produce the reference command notifications. It quantifies over every division of that input into pieces. The file relation includes the chosen version-switching and exit policies. The supplied declaration defines successful reading; it does not prove it for a particular reader.

BSmtLibSpec.Reader.FinishesOnlyOnFiles.text: If a reader finishes after its input has ended, the condition requires some command sequence for which that input satisfies the formal file relation. This is a recognition requirement, not a claim that those commands are well sorted or executed correctly. The declaration gives the desired implication for an arbitrary reader rather than establishing it for an implementation.

BSmtLibSpec.Reader.CallsDetermineCommand.text: Two admitted files producing identical command notifications must have the same initial version and command sequence. This condition concerns recovered commands, not the original bytes: whitespace, comments and the ignored suffix after exit are absent from notifications, and different older string spellings can have the same decoded content. The declaration defines the requirement; the authors' proof of it is shown as source with this page and was not compiled for it.

BSmtLibSpec.Reader.LexesThenParses.text: The formal definition requires a reader's observable results to agree with a lexer and parser satisfying their respective correctness conditions. The parser receives the decoded lexical tokens, and its callbacks determine the reader's output. Those lexer and parser conditions are assumptions inside this specification. The declaration is not a proof that the actual reader or any SMT solver satisfies them.
